title: Holiday Wedding Guest Dresses
metaTitle: Holiday Wedding Guest Dresses: December to New Year, Sorted
metaDescription: Holiday wedding guest dresses for December weddings, New Year's Eve and themed receptions. What the season permits, which fabrics work, and one dress for all three.
h1: Holiday Wedding Guest Dresses: Dressing the December-to-January Run
intro: Holiday wedding guest dresses have to cover more ground than any other season's, because the weeks between late November and early January hold three quite different events under one label. A December wedding is usually formal, often religious and frequently in daylight. A New Year's Eve wedding is a party that happens to include a ceremony. A holiday-themed reception takes its cue from the couple's own palette. This is the season that most rewards sparkle and depth of color, punishes thin summer fabrics, and catches guests out every year on the same two things: the coat and the shoes.

contentSections.heading: Which holiday wedding are you going to?
contentSections.content:
Work this out before you shop, because a dress that is perfect at one is noticeably wrong at another.

A December wedding is usually a formal winter wedding: often religious, often in the afternoon, family-heavy. Rich colors, heavier fabrics and sleeves suit it, and restraint reads well.

A New Year's Eve wedding is a party first. It runs late, it is often black tie or near it, and it is the one wedding of the year where full sequins, heavy metallics and real sparkle are pitched exactly right. A floor-length or high-shine dress that would overshoot a 2 p.m. church service is correct at a midnight countdown; plan shoes for dancing and a coat for a late, cold exit.

A holiday-themed reception sits in between and follows the couple's palette: evergreen and candlelight, red and gold, or a winter-white scheme (which is the couple's choice, not an invitation for guests to wear white).

A fourth case catches people out: a holiday destination wedding follows the destination's climate, not the calendar. A December wedding in Mexico or the Caribbean is a warm-weather wedding. Keep the seasonal palette if you like it, since a garnet or emerald dress in a light fabric still reads December, but choose chiffon, crepe de chine or light satin rather than velvet.

contentSections.heading: What "festive attire" means
contentSections.content:
Some holiday invitations say "festive attire." The Emily Post Institute's attire guide defines it as cocktail-party attire with a seasonal touch, usually for the holidays, and lists for women a cocktail dress, a long dressy skirt and top, a dressy pants outfit or separates, and a little black dress, with the note to "feature holiday colors."

In practice that means the formality of a cocktail party plus one seasonal signal: a jewel color, velvet, a metallic thread, a sequined top with a dressy skirt, or holiday jewelry. It does not mean costume. A Christmas-print dress or novelty accessories belong at an office party, not a wedding. For a wedding that is specifically Christmas-themed, the site's guide to what to wear to a Christmas wedding goes further.

contentSections.heading: Sparkle and color: what December allows
contentSections.content:
Holiday weddings loosen two constraints that apply the rest of the year.

Sparkle. Sequins, beading, lamé, metallic thread and high-shine satin read as seasonal rather than excessive between Thanksgiving and New Year's. A sequinned midi that would look like too much at an August garden wedding looks correct at a December evening reception.

Depth of color. Emerald, burgundy, garnet, plum, bottle green, midnight and black all come into their own, and so do metallic neutrals such as bronze, pewter and antique gold, which are hard to place in spring.

Red works best in deeper shades: wine, garnet and oxblood are some of the strongest December colors. Bright red paired with green tips from dressing into decoration at a reception already full of evergreen and berries. Black is entirely appropriate at an evening December reception; at an overtly Christmas-themed wedding a jewel tone joins in more warmly but is no more correct.

The couple's palette outranks all of this. Many holiday weddings publish a color scheme on the wedding website, and some couples ask guests to avoid a particular shade. Check before you buy.

contentSections.heading: Fabric, the ground and the cold
contentSections.content:
Velvet is the season's defining fabric: it holds deep color, photographs well in the warm, low, often candlelit light of a December reception, and it is warm. Satin, taffeta, brocade, jacquard, heavy crepe and beaded fabrics behave well in the same light. Thin chiffon, voile and light jersey look out of season and feel cold.

The outer layer gets forgotten every year. Holiday receptions mean moving between heated rooms and freezing parking lots, standing outside for photographs, and sometimes a sparkler send-off, often with no coat check. A tailored wool coat, a wrap coat or a faux-fur stole that sits cleanly over the dress is worth more than any accessory, so choose the dress with its coat in mind; strapless and elaborate-sleeved dresses are the hardest to cover.

The ground is the other problem. Frost, rain, gravel and wet grass defeat a stiletto. Block heels, wedges or a sleek ankle boot cope, and a boot under a midi in December looks deliberate.

contentSections.heading: Daytime December and church ceremonies
contentSections.content:
Daytime winter weddings are the case guests most often misjudge, because the calendar says party and the clock says otherwise. In late December much of the United States is dark by late afternoon, so a 2 p.m. ceremony and a 5 p.m. reception mean flat gray daylight for one and artificial light for the other. A mid-depth jewel tone in a fabric with some sheen, rather than full high-shine, photographs well in both.

Churches add two constraints. A stone building is cold for the time you sit still in it, and many expect covered shoulders and a hem at or below the knee. A velvet or crepe midi with long sleeves meets the temperature, the expectation and the season in one garment. Dress for the church, then remove a layer for the reception, not the other way around. The site's church wedding guest dress guide covers coverage in more detail.

contentSections.heading: One dress for the whole season, bought early
contentSections.content:
Many guests attend more than one event between December and January. The dress that covers the most ground is a jewel-tone midi with a defined waist, in velvet or satin-backed crepe, with sleeves or straps that take a coat. The accessories change the register: matte gold and a wool wrap read traditional for a Christmas wedding; high-shine metallics, a beaded clutch and a bolder lip read party for New Year's Eve.

Shop earlier than feels necessary. Occasion wear in velvet and sequins is a seasonal category, and the closer you get to the date, the fewer sizes and colors are likely to remain. Late-November sales can help, but only if there is still time for an exchange and a hem. Order two sizes of the dress you want rather than one size of three different dresses, since comparing fit is more useful than comparing options, and leave a week for a hem, because tailors are busy in December.

faqs.question: Are sequins appropriate at a holiday wedding?
faqs.answer: More than at any other time of year. At a New Year's Eve wedding, full sequin is the right pitch. At a daytime December wedding, sequin detailing or a beaded bodice reads better than head-to-toe sparkle.

faqs.question: What shoes work for a December wedding?
faqs.answer: Block heels, wedges or a sleek ankle boot. Frost, gravel and wet grass all defeat a stiletto, and a boot under a midi in winter reads as a styling choice. If the reception is indoors and you want delicate sandals, wear practical shoes to the venue and change there.

faqs.question: What should I wear over a holiday wedding dress?
faqs.answer: Bring a proper coat for arrivals, outdoor photographs and the exit: tailored wool, a wrap coat, or a faux-fur stole for shorter transfers. Choose one long enough to cover your hem if the dress is midi or longer, and check whether the venue has a coat check before deciding how bulky it can be.

heroImage.alt: Guests in floor-length gowns photographed in daylight

answer: Holiday wedding guest dresses are cocktail dresses, long dressy skirts with a top, dressy separates or a little black dress, in velvet, satin, brocade or sequins and in jewel tones, black or metallics. Emily Post calls this festive attire and suggests featuring holiday colors. Save full sequin for evening and New Year's Eve, and never wear winter white or ivory.
